One sample for several estimates

Source: vignettes/multivariate.Rmd
multivariate.Rmd

A survey rarely serves one estimate. An establishment survey wants revenue and employment; a school survey wants pupils and teachers. A size measure proportional to one variable is a poor size for the other, and drawing two samples costs twice. This vignette builds one sample that serves both, with the two tools the practice of Chromy’s method grew around it: the maximal size measure and the equal-CV allocation.

The maximal size measure

For each unit take its share of each auxiliary variable’s total, scale each share by how much sample that variable is to command, and let the unit’s size be the largest of its scaled shares (Folsom, Potter and Williams, 1987). Selecting proportional to the maximum guarantees every variable at least its intended coverage: a unit that matters for any variable is given the probability that variable needs.

library(chromy)
set.seed(2026)

frame <- data.frame(
  sector  = sample(c("manufacturing", "services", "trade"), 400,
                   replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.2, 0.5, 0.3)),
  revenue = rlnorm(400, meanlog = 6, sdlog = 1.4),
  workers = round(rlnorm(400, meanlog = 3, sdlog = 0.8))
)

size <- mpps_size(frame, c("revenue", "workers"))
head(cbind(frame, size))
#>     sector    revenue workers        size
#> 1    trade  220.33808      43 0.004073127
#> 2    trade  766.64788      17 0.001610306
#> 3 services  292.62948      20 0.001894478
#> 4 services   29.97168      30 0.002841716
#> 5    trade  268.93135      14 0.001326134
#> 6 services 4788.62088      17 0.010037309

The equal-CV allocation

The factors — how much sample each variable commands — are the design’s real lever. eqcv_allocation() searches for the factors under which every variable’s total is anticipated with the same coefficient of variation, so no estimate is quietly sacrificed to another: at each step the anticipated CVs are computed under the design the current factors imply, and the factors move against their spread until it closes.

n_j <- eqcv_allocation(frame, c("revenue", "workers"), n = 60)
n_j
#>   revenue   workers 
#> 1.0902054 0.9172584 
#> attr(,"cv")
#>    revenue    workers 
#> 0.05797872 0.05793798 
#> attr(,"iterations")
#> [1] 5
#> attr(,"converged")
#> [1] TRUE
attr(n_j, "cv")
#>    revenue    workers 
#> 0.05797872 0.05793798

The anticipated CVs match. Compare the factors a naive equal split would give — the skewed variable (revenue) needs more of the sample than the tame one:

attr(suppressWarnings(
  eqcv_allocation(frame, c("revenue", "workers"), n = 60, max_iterations = 0)
), "cv")
#>    revenue    workers 
#> 0.06446797 0.05074703

The design, in one call

chromy_sample() runs the allocation and the measure itself when given variables; n_j = "eqcv" is the default.

s <- chromy_sample(
  frame,
  n = 60, variables = c("revenue", "workers"),
  order_by = c("sector", "chromy_size"),
  seed = 7
)
s$n_j
#>   revenue   workers 
#> 1.0902054 0.9172584
estimate_total(s, c("revenue", "workers"))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   variable   total     se cv_pct random_draws
#>   <chr>      <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>        <int>
#> 1 revenue  443089. 36114.   8.15           55
#> 2 workers   10171.   770.   7.57           55
colSums(frame[c("revenue", "workers")])   # the true totals
#>  revenue  workers 
#> 477082.1  10557.0

Both totals are estimated from the one sample, each within its design’s reach, and the realised CVs sit where the anticipation put them — close to each other.

Fixed factors

When the factors are policy rather than search — a variable that must dominate, a historical allocation to keep — pass them directly:

s2 <- chromy_sample(
  frame,
  n = 60, variables = c("revenue", "workers"), n_j = c(2, 1),
  seed = 7
)
estimate_total(s2, c("revenue", "workers"))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   variable   total     se cv_pct random_draws
#>   <chr>      <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>        <int>
#> 1 revenue  478627. 23041.   4.81           55
#> 2 workers   11008.  1216.  11.0            55

References

Folsom, R. E., Potter, F. J. and Williams, S. R. (1987). Notes on a composite size measure for self-weighting samples in multiple domains. Proceedings of the American Statistical Association, Section on Survey Research Methods, 792–796.
